title: One small try, named
summary: Naming a try means picking one small action, what you hope to learn from it, and when you will stop.
body:
## What a try is

A try is one manageable action and a question it might answer. It is not a project, and it does not promise a result. This module has three moves: name the try, do the try, notice what it taught. You can Create, Practice, or Move forward. Create might be a rough sample. Practice might be one beginner task. Move forward might be reading real course requirements.

## Bounded beats big

"Spend fifteen minutes sketching on paper to see if I like arranging information" is more bounded than "Build a website." It has an action, a question, and a time limit. Nothing has to be finished. Planning only, watching a demonstration, or trying with help are all valid routes.

## The stop rule

Before you start, write what the try should teach, how big it is, when it ends, and what support you need. A stop rule says when to end or change the activity. It is part of the plan, not a sign you gave up. No payment, customer, public sharing, or second try is needed.

> Imagined example: "Try one beginner task from a class video, using paper and a pen I already own. Learning question: do I enjoy this kind of work? Limit: 15 minutes. Stop rule: if I feel stuck or tired, I stop and write down why."
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Doing it inside your limits
summary: Doing the try means following your plan, not proving how much you can push through.
body:
## Check the plan first

Before you begin, look again at your learning question, the size of the try, the time limit, and the stop rule. If something you need is missing, you can change the plan or write down that it did not happen. That is an accurate record.

## Honest records

"Tool unavailable; task not attempted" is a useful note. It does not say whether you would enjoy the task. It does say what would have to change before you could find out. Trying with support counts just as much as trying alone. Watching a demonstration is different from doing, so say which one you did.

## No pushing

Do not stretch the task to get a better result. If you reach the stop rule, stop or change the activity as you planned, and note what is unfinished. If another question comes up, save it for later. No bigger second try is needed in this session.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Taught, cost, still unknown
summary: A try review asks three different questions and ends with a choice you can change.
body:
## Three questions

What did it teach? What did it cost? What is still unknown? These are separate. A try can be useful without being fun, finished, or worth repeating. "I enjoyed arranging the pieces, needed help with instructions, and felt tired afterward" gives you more than "it went well."

## Words or ratings

Plain words are enough. If you like, note enjoyment and whether you did what you planned as two separate things. Optional ratings are for you. They are not measures of anything, not readiness scores, and not proof that anyone wants what you made.

## What to do next

If your try included an invitation or offer, you can write Yes, No, Maybe, or no response. That describes this invitation only, not what a whole market wants. Then choose: keep, change, test again, park, stop, redirect, or leave open. Continue Looking is a full decision. You do not need another try to finish.

> Imagined example: "Taught: I liked arranging the pieces. Cost: about 20 minutes and I felt tired. Unknown: whether the instructions would be easier with a person nearby. Next: park it for now."
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: A simple cost map
summary: A cost map shows money and resources tied to one step, including when the amount is zero.
body:
## What it is

A cost map connects money with one try or next step you really considered. It is not a financial history and not a business plan. A $0 try, a plan-only case, or a made-up example is enough to practice. Educational only: this is not financial, legal, or tax advice.

## Five things

Spent: money you paid. Received: money that came in, if any. Owned: things you already had. Borrowed: things you used with permission that belong to someone else. Forgotten: costs you missed at first. "No new materials bought" does not mean no resources were used. Leave unknown amounts unknown.

## In vs kept

Money that came in is not the same as money kept. If a made-up try brings in $20 and had $8 in direct costs, $12 is left after those listed costs. That is a simple sum. It leaves out time, taxes, and other expenses. Keep project money apart from household information, and share only what the decision needs. No bank statements or account numbers are needed.

> Imagined example, matching the app's neutral case: someone sells six handmade cards at $5 each, so $30 comes in. They spent $12 on cardstock and $6 on bus fare, so $12 is kept, not $30. Owned: scissors and pens. Borrowed: a friend's printer. Forgotten at first: about three hours of time.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Labour, limits, and a boundary
summary: Money totals miss time, effort and help, so count those too and name what a step must not risk.
body:
## Count the work

A money total can miss much of what a step takes. Time, preparation, travel, mistakes, emotional energy, rest afterward, and help from others all count, including unpaid help. You do not need to invent an hourly wage to see that work has a cost. A "free" workshop may still mean travel, childcare, two hours there, and time to recover. This is not financial advice.

## Real constraints

You can name constraints without sharing your history: schedule, transport, access, credentials, childcare. These are not measures of commitment. Ask whose action could change a barrier. Some limits you choose to protect. Others belong to a program, workplace, or service, such as an inaccessible location. You do not have to solve every obstacle alone.

## A boundary

An affordability boundary says what the next step must not put at risk, for example rent, a work shift, health, rest, or a responsibility you choose. You can state it without giving amounts. Share only what this decision needs. If a question goes further, you can stop.

> Imagined example: "This step must not cost me a work shift or my rest on days I care for family. I will not borrow for it." No amounts are given.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Three equal paths
summary: You can use what you counted to choose a next step, and pausing is a full choice.
body:
## Honest, not certain

A financially honest choice uses the costs and limits you can see. You do not need to know every future expense. Ask: can I afford this particular step, do I need income now, what would repeating it need, and what would have to change? An unpaid try might not be repeatable next to paid work. What you learned still counts.

## Three equal paths

Pathway: employment, training, a trade, stability, or the practical cost of another life step. Project or offer: cost out one more bounded step, only if it is still worth looking into. Pause or Continue Looking: protect essentials and put no more attention or money here for now. Paid work is not quitting. Pausing is not weak passion. A project does not win just because it sounds like business.

## Keep your boundary

Carry your affordability boundary into the choice and keep unknown costs visible. This is educational, not financial, debt, tax, or benefits advice. Those questions need a qualified source, and a referral may not be available yet. You do not have to move on to the next module or start another try.

> Imagined example: "The card sale taught me I like making them. It brought in $30 and I kept $12, plus three hours of time. My boundary is my work shifts. Choice: Pause for now, and look at paid work."
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Success-now: a standard for the next step
summary: Success-now is a practical yardstick for your next choice, built from what you actually tried and learned.
body:
## What success-now means

Success-now describes what a useful next step would look like under your current conditions. It is not a life goal. It is not a verdict on your future. Your sense of meaning or purpose can grow, stay unclear, or change. You do not need to settle it before you decide something small and practical.

## Look at your records, not your life story

You do not need to write an autobiography. Use what you already saved. Ask five short questions. What did I think? What did I try? What happened? What did I learn? What changed? Include the evidence you would rather not see, as well as the evidence that backs the direction you like. Both count.

## Four words that are not the same

Passion, inspiration, purpose, and success are different things. Interest does not guarantee access. Feeling inspired does not pay for anything. Lack of money, time, or transport is a barrier in the world. It is not a sign that you lack passion. A good next choice can protect your stability even if no clear passion shows up.

## Write it without a should

Try writing your success-now in your own words, with no "should" in it. The next step might be work, training, a project, a pause, or more looking. All of those are fine. You do not need a destiny, a trauma story, or a deep personal tale. "I don't know yet" can be part of the statement.

> Imagined example (not a real person): At the start, someone wrote, "Launch something of my own." After looking at their records, they wrote, "Know whether this question is worth another small try without missing rent." Neither statement is wrong. The second one was updated by evidence. It is a yardstick for the next choice, not a destiny.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Direction cards: a choice for now
summary: A direction card helps you organise today's choice; it does not give you an identity.
body:
## Three cards, equal weight

A direction card is a way to organise a choice you are making now. There are three. Work or training. Project, venture, or creative offer. Stabilise, pause, or keep looking. They have equal standing. A job is not a fallback from a venture. A pause is not a failed search for purpose. You can think about more than one card, or stay unsure.

## Entrepreneurship is one option

Starting something of your own can fit inside the second card. It is one option, not the point of the program. Helping others or giving back can fit inside any card if you want it. It is not an extra requirement. You can also choose none of these today.

## Two questions for any direction

For the direction you are looking at, ask two things. What is it allowed to ask of me? What is it not allowed to cost me? Bring in the limits you set in the cost review. Time, energy, access, support, uncertainty, and responsibilities belong next to interest. A structural barrier says something about the situation. It says nothing bad about your commitment.

## A workable next position

Good answers are small and name a limit. "Explore a course while protecting my current shifts" is one. "Pause while I check transport options" is another. Both are real decisions. You are choosing a workable next position, not a permanent label. You can change your card when things change.

> Imagined example (not a real person): The card is Work or training. It is allowed to ask for two evenings a week. It is not allowed to cost the Saturday shift that covers rent.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: A record you can come back to
summary: The Current Direction Record holds one next action, what it might teach you, and when you will look again.
body:
## What continuity means

Continuity means leaving yourself a clear note about the choice you are making now, so you can return to it and change it. The Current Direction Record is not a second project. It is not a permanent identity. It holds what you are choosing today and why.

## Four questions

Answer four short questions. What am I doing next? Why does this make sense, given what I have learned? What might it teach me? When, or under what condition, will I look at it again? A review point can be a date. It can also be an event, like getting a piece of information.

## Small and checkable

A small, checkable record beats a big plan. For example: "I will check the course timetable, because schedule was the main barrier. I want to learn whether an accessible option exists. I will review after I have that answer." That is easier to act on than a five-year plan.

## Keep the unknowns visible

If you are still looking, name what you don't know and when you will look again. If you are pausing, say what the pause protects. Do not make up an action just so the record looks full. Your limits and uncertainty can stay on the page. You can change the record whenever things change.

> Imagined example (not a real person): Next action: ask the college if an evening class exists. Why: schedule was the barrier. What it might teach me: whether this option is possible at all. Review: when I hear back.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: What we share, and what we don't have to
summary: The group shares a practice, not one approved destination, and every path belongs.
body:
## A shared practice

What this group shares is a practice: noticing, trying, reflecting, and deciding. It does not share one approved destination. Work, training, a project or venture, a pause, more looking, and leaving all belong. Someone who takes a job, or never finds a clear passion, is not a lesser member.

## No ranking of paths

Doing more activities does not give anyone say over another person's private choices. Two people can learn from the same session and decide differently. One keeps a project going. One sets it aside to protect a work schedule. They can still swap useful observations. Neither choice is a failure.

## Norms that make it possible

A few habits keep this safe. Ask before giving feedback. Pass when you want to. Allow disagreement. Respect privacy. Let people change their minds or leave. Belonging does not mean taking advice, sharing a story, or staying in touch forever.

## Say as little or as much as you like

You can describe who you are now in a few words. You can also choose not to introduce yourself at all. No hardship story is an admission ticket. Shared identity here is an invitation to practice together. It is not a label you must wear.

> Imagined example (not real people): Sam and Jo hear the same session. Sam keeps working on a project. Jo parks hers to keep her work hours. Next time, they each share one thing they noticed. Nobody asks who chose better.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: A connection map: ideas, not promises
summary: A connection map is a draft of how the group might stay in touch, with each item marked proposed or available.
body:
## What a connection map is

A connection map is a draft of how this group might stay in touch. It is separate from anyone's private Life Map. Its job is to make expectations clear. It does not create a duty to stay active. Each person still chooses whether, how, and when to stay connected.

## Three practical questions

Talk through three things. How often do people want contact? Which channels can people actually use? Which group habits are worth keeping? Earlier habits like asking permission, listening, passing, and giving limited feedback can come along. None of them needs personal disclosure.

## Proposed or available

Mark every item as proposed or available. "Monthly online check-in: proposed, no host confirmed" is honest. "Monthly check-in: available, with a confirmed host and channel" is different. An idea does not become a service because it is on the map. Nothing is available until someone has actually set it up.

## What a channel asks of you

Every channel asks something. A device, data, an account, visible contact details, or time. Do not assume everyone can or wants to use it. Agree what can be shared, and how someone can step back. A group preference does not sign anyone up.

> Imagined example (not a real group): 'Group chat: proposed, needs a phone number from everyone, so maybe not. Monthly call: proposed, no host yet. Shared notes page: proposed, nobody has agreed to keep it up.' All three are ideas for now.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Your place is a choice about contact
summary: You choose how close to stay, what to agree to, and you can change it later.
body:
## Three equal options

Your place in the group is a choice about contact. It is not a measure of loyalty. The options are Stay close, Light touch, and Private or pause. Stay close is active connection. Light touch is occasional updates, where those truly exist. Private or pause is no contact, or contact later. Any next direction fits any option.

## Only what exists

Events or yearly check-ins that are only proposed are not promises. Light touch can only mean something real once someone has set it up. Someone can take a job and choose light touch. Someone else can keep a project going and choose privacy. Neither choice says how much this mattered to them.

## Roles, if you want one

If the group sets roles up, a role could be a host, a peer witness, or a resource sharer. A role needs a clear scope, an end date, and a way to stop. It does not make you a mentor, a counsellor, or unpaid staff. A community peer role is not peer counselling. "None" and "not now" are complete answers.

## Four separate permissions

Follow-up, media, evaluation, and events are four separate choices. Each one is Yes, No, or Not now. Saying yes to one does not mean yes to another. You can change any of them later. No public story, regular attendance, continuing a venture, or automatic alumni sign-up is needed.

> Imagined example (not a real person): Ana picks Light touch. Follow-up: Not now. Media: No. Evaluation: Yes. Events: Not now. Role: none. She can change any of these next month.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)
